source.title: Scaling Laws for Neural Material Models
source.authors: Akshay Trikha; K. Chu; Advait Gosai; Parker Szachta; E. Weiner

record.file_problem: None noted; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: Tests empirical scaling relationships in neural models for material-property prediction, extending scaling-law investigations to a different domain and model setting.
record.gate_note: The paper reports its own validation-loss scaling results for dataset size, parameter count, and compute. It does not test language-model pretraining loss or extrapolation from small runs to much larger runs. Training-speed and mixed-precision results are not rows because they do not measure the claimed loss scaling.
record.test_reason: The study fits its own power laws of validation loss against data, parameters and FLOPs for EquiformerV2 and Transformer models predicting material properties on OMat24. This is a new setting outside text pretraining, so it bears on V5. It does not test language-model loss, extrapolation, compute-optimal allocation, shape at fixed parameters or downstream tasks.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors report power-law scaling for EquiformerV2 across data, parameters and compute. Transformers have much smaller exponents, show no learning below 10^15 FLOPs, and reach a loss floor about 8× higher. The authors attribute the gap to the physical-symmetry inductive biases built into EquiformerV2.
record.recipe_differences: Uses material-property prediction with OMat24 and reports validation loss for Transformers and EquiformerV2, rather than language-model pretraining cross-entropy. It does not reproduce the original language-model training setup.
record.method_sensitivity: Architecture affects reported scaling behavior; the EquiformerV2 compute fit improves when noisy validation losses from the first few epochs are removed.

fits_no_version.finding: Fitted scaling exponents differ sharply by architecture in the same domain. EquiformerV2 has data and parameter exponents of 0.242 and 0.383. Transformers have 0.052 and 0.120. The authors attribute this to equivariant inductive biases.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In non-language domains, scaling exponents depend strongly on the architecture's inductive biases.

record.problems: The paper reports insufficient results to demonstrate successful Transformer dataset scaling and insufficient data for fool-proof Transformer compute-scaling laws. It reports no uncertainty estimates for the scaling fits, and notes validation-loss volatility, a model-initialization anomaly, and high-compute flattening.

untested.parts: Image and video models, repeated data, fine-tuning and transfer are not tested. Only material-property models on OMat24 are covered. The intro's claimed range of 10^2 to 10^9 parameters is not reflected in the reported fits: EquiformerV2 goes up to about 2M and Transformers up to about 9M.
Not tested: no language-model held-out loss.
Not tested: no small-to-large prediction is checked.
Not tested: no allocation under a fixed compute budget.
Not tested: there is no fixed-parameter shape sweep. Parameters are scaled mostly via depth.
Not tested for language-model laws. There is no systematic variation of parameter counting, schedule, data or fitting method.

missing.what: Transformers needed about 10× more compute than EquiformerV2 to reach sufficient loss values.
EquiformerV2 models below 10^14 FLOPs fail to reach loss under 20. The steepest improvement is at 10^14–10^15 FLOPs, so the curve is not a single straight line across the full range.

record.verdict_notes: This is a student-style preprint. No uncertainty is reported on any fit. The numbers of points per fit and the dataset-size ranges are not stated. Training-speed and mixed-precision results are correctly excluded as rows. V7 links were removed because architecture-dependent exponents in a materials domain are not the setup and fitting choices V7 names; that finding is recorded under fits_no_version.

versions.untested_parts: Tests neither language-model held-out cross-entropy nor parameter, token, or compute scaling in language models.
Fits scaling relationships but does not report predictions from small runs evaluated against runs orders of magnitude larger.
Does not optimize parameter and token allocations under a fixed compute budget or report compute-optimal allocations.
Compares architectures, but does not report a controlled comparison of depth, width, or other architecture details at a fixed parameter count.
Tests material-property prediction models trained on OMat24; does not test image or video models, repeated data, fine-tuning, or transfer.
Does not measure downstream-task performance or its predictability from scale or pretraining loss.
Does not compare parameter-counting methods, training schedules, or data choices systematically, nor test disagreement among published language-model laws or compute-optimal allocations.

rows.subject: EquiformerV2
rows.operation_detail: Varied training dataset size and fit validation loss as a power law.
rows.note: The paper identifies this as its most representative EquiformerV2 architecture.
rows.check: V7 link removed. One architecture's fitted exponent does not show that exponents depend on setup or fitting choices in the sense V7 names. No uncertainty is given, and the dataset-size range is not stated.

rows.subject: Transformer
rows.operation_detail: Varied training dataset size and fit validation loss as a power law.
rows.note: The paper also says there were insufficient results to demonstrate successful Transformer scaling.
rows.check: V7 link removed. The paper writes the variable as N, but this is the dataset-scaling sweep, so it is data size. The authors say they have insufficient results to demonstrate successful Transformer scaling. The exponent of 0.052 is very weak.

rows.subject: Transformer models (aggregate)
rows.operation_detail: Varied training dataset size; the paper reports a plateau across most tested models.
rows.note: Aggregate result for most tested models; models with parameter counts of 2–9M were reported to break past this barrier.
rows.check: The subject and size are misattributed. The plateau at 40 applies to most tested Transformers. The 2–9M-parameter models are the ones that break past it. For the plateaued models there is no scaling (see r10: they output zero forces), so the state is absent, not partial.

rows.subject: EquiformerV2
rows.operation_detail: Varied parameter count with training data fixed at 100K samples.
rows.check: V7 link removed. P is non-embedding parameters. The measure is fit on 100K samples, and the text does not say whether the fit is to train or validation loss.

rows.subject: EquiformerV2
rows.operation_detail: Compared a model's train and validation losses with the parameter-scaling trend.

conditions.value: particular model; initialization identified as a random bad case

rows.measure: Training and validation loss relative to trend
rows.value: Both losses deviate from the trend
rows.note: The authors attribute the deviation to a random bad case of model initialization.
rows.check: This is a single-model anomaly that the authors attribute to bad initialization. It is marginal as a result row and does not change the EquiformerV2 parameter trend.

rows.subject: Transformer
rows.operation_detail: Varied parameter count with training data fixed at 100K samples.
rows.note: The paper reports the fit for 100K samples and separately notes validation overfitting on low amounts of data.
rows.check: V7 link removed. The exponent of 0.120 is weak. There are insufficient data at 300K, and validation loss overfits at low data.

rows.subject: Transformer
rows.operation_detail: Compared training and validation losses while varying parameter count.
rows.value: Training loss follows a predictable trend; models overfit, as shown by validation loss
rows.check: None beyond its overlap with r6.

rows.subject: EquiformerV2 models (Pareto frontier aggregate)
rows.operation_detail: Tracked compute in FLOPs and fit validation loss against compute.
rows.value: Decreased from approximately 50 to 3; L ≈ 4.99 · 10^5 · C^-0.339
rows.note: The paper describes the loss decrease across four orders of magnitude of compute.
rows.check: V7 link removed. The frontier spans 10^13–10^17 FLOPs, and loss falls from about 50 to 3.

rows.subject: EquiformerV2 models (Pareto frontier aggregate)
rows.operation_detail: Examined the high-compute region of the validation-loss frontier.
rows.value: Frontier begins to flatten; larger compute investments yield increasingly marginal improvements
rows.check: V7 link removed. The flattening above 10^16 FLOPs is a qualitative statement with no numbers. It bears on how far the material-domain power law holds.

rows.subject: Transformer models (aggregate)
rows.operation_detail: Measured validation loss across compute levels.
rows.measure: Validation loss and evidence of learning
rows.value: Most models plateau at validation loss 40; the paper says they set forces to 0 regardless of input and demonstrate no actual learning
rows.note: Aggregate result for most models under the stated compute regime.
rows.check: None. The authors attribute the plateau to parameter and data constraints, which are bottlenecks the version excludes.

rows.subject: Transformer models
rows.operation_detail: Measured validation loss at high compute.
rows.baseline: EquiformerV2 validation loss approximately 3 in the high-compute comparison
rows.value: Lowest validation loss around 25; approximately 8× higher than EquiformerV2
rows.check: The comparison is between architectures at matched compute, not a scaling measurement in itself. It is kept as context for the weak Transformer scaling.

rows.subject: EquiformerV2 models (compute curves aggregate)
rows.operation_detail: Compared the compute-curve fit with and without noisy validation losses from the first few epochs.

conditions.value: first few epochs included versus removed

rows.baseline: Fit including noise from the first few epochs
rows.value: Fit improves when the noise from the first few epochs is removed
rows.check: This concerns fit quality after dropping early-epoch noise. No changed exponent or goodness-of-fit number is reported, and it is not a language-model scaling-law fitting choice of the kind V7 names.

relationships.condition: EquiformerV2 on OMat24, scaling data, non-embedding parameters or compute
relationships.reason: Power-law fits are reported for each sweep: D^-0.242 (r1), P^-0.383 (r4), and C^-0.339 across four orders of compute (r8). No uncertainty is given.
relationships.display_finding: Loss fits scale as D^-0.242, P^-0.383, and C^-0.339 across four orders of compute, without reported uncertainty.

relationships.reason: The Pareto frontier flattens, with increasingly marginal gains at the highest compute (r9). There is also one initialization outlier (r5).
relationships.display_finding: The Pareto frontier flattened above 10¹⁶ FLOPs, with increasingly marginal gains and an initialization outlier.

relationships.condition: Encoder-only Transformers on OMat24 (2–9M parameters, up to 300K samples)
relationships.reason: Most models plateau at loss 40 with no learning below 10^15 FLOPs (r3, r10). Where fits exist, the exponents are weak (0.052 for data, 0.120 for parameters; r2, r6), with overfitting (r7) and a loss about 8× above EquiformerV2 (r11). The authors call the data insufficient and blame data and parameter bottlenecks.
relationships.display_finding: Most transformers plateaued near loss 40 without learning below 10¹⁵ FLOPs; fitted data and parameter exponents were 0.052 and 0.120, with overfitting and loss about eight times EquiformerV2's.
